Chapter 3: The Consequences of Not Knowing About Religion
Have you ever thought about what happens when we don’t really understand religion—not just as an academic subject, but as something that shapes our daily lives?
When people lack even the basics about the world’s religions—their beliefs, practices, and histories—it’s not just theory. It spills over into our conversations, our communities, and even our democracy.
Here’s where it shows up first: public discussions. Think about the times you’ve heard politicians reference biblical stories or activists quote religious leaders. It happens all the time, right? But if we don’t know the stories—like the meaning behind being a “Good Samaritan”—the whole point can be lost or twisted. Suddenly, important conversations become shallow, or worse, completely misunderstood.
The same thing happens in the media. Journalists report on religious events or controversies, but often without the right background. So, stories about conflicts in the Middle East, debates over religious freedom, or the rise of new religious movements end up oversimplified. Sometimes, they even reinforce harmful stereotypes. That not only misinforms us—it can actually add fuel to prejudice and division.
Now, let’s talk about democracy. We live in a country with people from every imaginable faith, and we’re all expected to help make decisions about laws and public policies. But if we don’t understand the basics of each other’s religions, how can we make fair choices? Just look at debates about religious symbols, holidays, or even things like teaching evolution in schools. Without knowledge, it’s almost impossible to craft policies that are truly just and effective.
And on a more personal level? Not knowing about someone’s dietary restrictions, the meaning behind a holiday, or why a friend practices a certain ritual can lead to awkward moments—or even offense. In workplaces, schools, and neighborhoods, this lack of understanding can chip away at trust and respect, making it harder to connect and work together.
The stakes get even higher when we look at global affairs. Around the world, religious conflict and cooperation shape international relationships. If we mix up the difference between Sunni and Shia Muslims, or miss the religious context in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, we risk making costly mistakes—and missing out on chances for peace.
There’s also the impact on education. If students graduate without a basic grasp of the world’s religions, they’re not really ready for the diverse society they’re stepping into. They’ll struggle to understand the forces shaping history, current events, and the people around them. It limits their ability to think critically, empathize, and really take part in civic life.
And here’s the thing: these effects aren’t just limited to a single group or one part of the country. They ripple across every community, every sector, everywhere. Fixing this problem is about more than just memorizing a few facts about religion. It means rethinking how we understand and teach it—seeing religious literacy as something that lifts us all up.
When we recognize what’s at stake, we start to see the real value of learning about religion. It’s not just about avoiding awkward moments or misunderstandings—it’s about building a stronger, more connected society, one that truly works for everyone.
